analytic.title: QoS Guarantee Using Probabilistic Deadlines

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: This paper presents a probabilistic approach to guarantee the performance of a real-time system. While traditional real-time system analysis tends to guarantee that each task instance will complete its execution before its absolute deadline (hard guarantee), our approach permits to estimate the probability that it will happen.

Such a statistical guarantee is performed based on interarrival and execution times probability distributions, rather than their worst case values. The advantage of a probabilistic approach is a more efficient usage of system resources, allowing to give a certain level of deadline guarantee to task sets that the classical schedulability analysis would reject.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Real-time activities are traditionally characterized by temporal constraints, called deadlines [17]. Each task is a stream of jobs Â , where Â is released at time Ö , is characterized by a computation time , and must finish before its absolute deadline . Depending on the consequence of a deadline miss, a real-time task is said to be hard, soft, or firm.

A hard task cannot tolerate any deadline miss, since a single job that finishes after its deadline could jeopardize the entire system. A soft task can tolerate jobs that finish after their deadlines, whereas a firm task can tolerate only some job failure. Typically, a firm job should either finish before its deadline or not execute at all. In other words, a soft job that misses its deadline can still do some useful work, while a firm job that misses its deadline is useless, though it does not jeopardize the system.

Due to their criticality, hard real-time tasks must be guaranteed off-line based on their Worst Case Execution Time (WCET) and Minimum Interarrival Time (MIT). If a hard task is accepted, each of its jobs is guaranteed to finish before its deadline. Firm tasks are generally subject to on-line admission test, so a job is released only if it is guaranteed to complete before its deadline, otherwise it is rejected.

Soft tasks are often accepted in the system without any form of guarantee. In order not to jeopardize hard tasks' schedulability, soft tasks can be served in background with respect to hard and firm tasks or, to improve responsiveness, by an aperiodic server, which can be used both under static priority assignment [14,21,13], and dynamic priority assignment [23,6,22]. When an aperiodic sever is used to handle soft tasks, the mean response time can be reduced, but in general it is difficult to guarantee the performance of each single task. In fact, typically, th objective of an aperiodic server is to reduce the mean response time, rather than meeting individual timing constraints. A possible (but inefficient) solution for handling soft tasks characterized by timing constraints is to treat them as hard or firm real-time tasks.

A firm task model can be a good trade-off between hard and soft models, since it permits to guarantee that each accepted job will finish before its deadline. In this way it is possible to achieve a higher CPU utilization, while providing a certain level of guarantee on non-hard tasks. In general, it is possible to ensure a Quality of Service (QoS) based on the maximum number of consecutive skips, the minimum distance between two skips [12,18], or the completion probability [2]. In [4,3], the bandwidth saved by skipped jobs is exploited for enhancing aperiodic responsiveness.
Summarizing, classical schedulability tests require the exact knowledge of the WCET, Ñ Ü , and the MIT,

This model can cause an underutilization of the CPU if the MIT is much smaller than the mean interarrival time, or the WCET is much greater than the mean execution time.

In many practical real-time applications, the requirements for a task are less stringent than real-time theory usually permits. A more flexible approach can be to specify the deadline completion probability: for example, a task can still be acceptable if the probability of respecting a deadline is greater than a given value.
In [24], a probabilistic analysis of the Rate Monotonic (RM) scheduling algorithm is performed, and some solutions to guarantee a completion probability are presented.

In [2], the RM algorithm is modified to perform on-line acceptance of single jobs for ensuring (off line) a minimum probability that a job is accepted; these two works are both limited to a static priority (RM) assignment and to a semiperiodic (fixed interarrival times) task model.

In [10], a Time Division Multiplexing (TDM) model is used to share resources between tasks in a distributed system. In this paper and in two successive works ( [11,9]) a statistical approach is used at design phase to compute the probability distribution of tasks' finishing times and to check whether a distributed system verifies some given constraints on latency and minimum output rate.

In [15] a statistical analysis of the Earliest Deadline First (EDF) scheduling algorithm is presented. This analysis is based on the Real-Time Queuing theory, which adapts the classical queuing theory to handle queues containing clients characterized by a deadline. Other works study EDF from a probabilistic point of view: for example, [19,7] prove that EDF possesses certain optimality properties minimizing lateness probabilities.

The use of a firm task model can be useful for solving this underutilization problem in the presence of relaxed (non-hard) tasks, but it still requires the a-priori knowledge of jobs' execution times. This problem makes firm tasks useless each time that the execution times cannot be exactly estimated. Another problem with the firm model is that jobs that cannot be guaranteed are rejected, though they could give some value also finishing after their deadline.

This problem can be addressed by adopting a soft task model, while using the completion probability as a metric for expressing and guaranteeing a desired QoS. While the aim of the classical hard schedulability analysis is to guarantee that each job will finish within its deadline, the aim of a QoS guarantee is to ensure that a job will finish within its soft deadline with a given probability. To perform a QoS guarantee we need to describe the tasks' parameters in a probabilistic way and introduce the concept of probabilistic deadline.
According to this approach, each task is described by a pair of Probability Distribution Functions (PDF):

div.head: Scheduling Model
div.p: Our work can be considered an extension of classical real-time scheduling. Conventional real-time systems schedule tasks by period (Rate Monotonic) [17], by relative deadlines (Deadline Monotonic) [16], or by absolute deadlines (Earliest Deadline First) [17]. This scheduling framework is acceptable for hard real-time activities, but it is too inefficient for soft real-time systems. For example, in a multimedia application the WCET and the MIT of the task cannot always be precisely estimated, and in many cases these parameters have a large variance.

On the other hand, performing the analysis using average values (rather than worst case ones) is not safe, because a misbehaved task would affect the execution of other tasks, causing them to miss their deadlines.

This problem can be solved by using a bandwidth reservation strategy: each task is assigned a fraction of the CPU bandwidth and the scheduling mechanism ensures that it will not require more than the reserved bandwidth. In this way, a task demanding too much time is just delayed, and cannot compromise the QoS guaranteed for the others; its worst-case finishing time only depends on its load.

Although any scheduling algorithm could be used in order to implement a reservation strategy (for example, in [20] a static priority assignment, derived from DM, is used to implement Processor Capacity Reserve), we decided to use a dynamic priority scheduler, based on EDF, to achieve better CPU utilization. Each soft task is handled by a dedicated Constant Bandwidth Server (CBS) [1]. The server mechanism assigns each job an initial deadline, which guarantees the reserved bandwidth Í × . The bandwidth isolation property is achieved by postponing the assigned deadline each time the task is demanding more than the reserved bandwidth. The server is described by two parameters É × and Ì × , where É × is the server budget and Ì × is the server period ( É× Ì× is the server bandwidth).
When a new request arrives, the server checks whether it can be scheduled using the last assigned deadline, otherwise the request is assigned an initial deadline equal to Ö • Ì × .
Each time the job executes for É × time units, its scheduling deadline is postponed by Ì × (in [1] a complete description of the algorithm can be found).

div.head: Design Issues
div.p: The presented method can be used at a design stage to assign the ´É× Ì × µ parameters to a CBS server. A correct definition of the server parameters should follow the steps outlined below:
1. Task model: the PDFs Í ´ µ and Î ´Øµ are found. They can be histograms collected through experiments or closed form functions that approximate the real distributions.
2. Task constraints definition: the designer assigns the ´AE Ô µ constraints to the tasks.

3. Statistical analysis: based on the task's parameters (Í ´ µ Î ´Øµ), the tool calculates the server characteristics that is a set of curves showing how ´AEµ changes as a function of the server parameters.
4. Parameter setting: the designer finds the ´AE Ô µ point on the server characteristics and selects the corresponding server parameters.

div.p: A full design methodology for distributed real-time systems can be found in [10,11,9]. In these papers, the authors show how to allocate resources in a distributed pipeline in order to meet some constraints like the input-output delay and the minimum output rate. The design process is based on partitioning the resources between tasks and using a probabilistic approach to check whether the constraints are respected. This step is repeated iteratively in order to find an adequate resource allocation.

div.head: Conclusions
div.p: In this paper, we showed how to perform QoS guarantee using probabilistic deadlines, when a Constant Bandwidth Server mechanism is used for soft tasks scheduling.
Our method has been formally analyzed and validated through intensive simulation, showing how it permits to achieve a desired QoS with better system utilization.
As a future work, we want to extend the proposed method to more general situations, in which both interarrival and execution times are randomly distributed.

Moreover, the proposed method has been tested, but not yet utilized in practical situations: as a future work, we plan to use it in a design phase (off-line guarantee) and check if it is usable for run time resource management (on-line QoS guarantee). In this case, we need a method for automatically deriving the interarrival and execution times PDFs at run time, using system measurements as a feedback.
